title: Charging and Discharging a Hubbard-Holstein Quantum Battery: Specific Mechanisms and General Insights
authors: Emil Östberg, Arvid Steen, Najmeh Abiri, Irene D'Amico, Claudio Verdozzi
abstract: A Hubbard-Holstein dimer functions as a correlation-driven quantum battery, with ergotropy robustly stored, under some conditions, even in the presence of dissipation. We find that, although optimal work extraction can in principle recover all the stored energy, it requires unrealistically fine-tuned couplings. By contrast, a physically realizable protocol based on spectral matching between the battery and the load achieves substantial, albeit suboptimal, energy extraction. Our results identify a mechanism for quantum energy storage, provide a realistic route to work extraction that is amenable to machine-learning-based theoretical exploration, and suggest that quantum batteries may not be universally deployable: the microscopic mechanism responsible for storing energy can constrain the classes of systems able to efficiently extract it.
summary: This paper analyzes a Hubbard-Holstein dimer as a quantum battery, demonstrating that while ideal work extraction is theoretically difficult, a practical protocol involving spectral matching can efficiently extract stored energy. The mechanism relies on the interplay between electronic correlations and phonon modes, offering insights into realistic quantum energy storage limitations.
main_problem: The research investigates efficient quantum energy storage and work extraction from a quantum battery, specifically addressing the gap between ideal theoretical protocols and physically realizable methods.
main_result: While optimal work extraction requires unphysical fine-tuning, a practical protocol based on spectral matching using phonon coupling allows for substantial, realistic energy extraction.
method: The study uses time evolution simulations governed by an extended Hubbard-Holstein Hamiltonian coupled to a dissipative bath, employing the mixed quantum–classical Ehrenfest approximation.
model_or_system: The system is a two-electron Hubbard–Holstein (HH) dimer acting as a quantum battery. It models electronic correlations (Hubbard term), electron-phonon coupling (Holstein term), and environmental dissipation via a Caldeira-Leggett bath.
key_observables: Ergotropy ($W$), site occupations ($\langle\hat{n}_Langle, \langle\hat{n}_Rangle$), and average phonon displacement ($\langle\hat{b}^\dagger + \hat{b}angle$).
important_parameters: The interplay between electronic coupling ($J$), on-site repulsion ($U$), and the spectral bandwidth of the bath.
main_assumptions: Ideal work extraction protocols often rely on unphysical, highly structured couplings; the use of the Ehrenfest approximation is noted as a limitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup (isolated vs. dissipative), time evolution showing phonon displacement and site occupations across charging, dissipation, and discharging regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the HH dimer as a quantum battery, contrasting ideal unitary discharge protocols with practical load-coupled methods, and analyzing how spectral matching dictates efficient energy retrieval while discussing the role of phonons in suppressing dissipation.
why_interesting: It bridges concepts from strongly correlated electron models (Hubbard) with open quantum systems dynamics (phonon coupling/dissipation), providing concrete mechanisms for non-equilibrium energy management relevant to quantum thermodynamics.
